doc.title: Mike Longo interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 13, 2019

title: Who Longo won't play with, and time in jazz
summary: He won't play with those who pay too little or can't swing; discusses free jazz and bebop drummers' time.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: What makes you not want to work with a particular musician?

Two things. They ain’t paying enough money. And the second thing is they can’t swing. And so, but I don’t run into that that much in New York man, I mean you know — back when I was coming up that was a must. If you couldn’t swing you wasn’t supposed to be © Fillius Jazz Archive -16-
up on the bandstand. Now today they make a style out of not swinging. That’s the new saying. Free jazz and all this other.
It’s like playing tennis without a net.
Yes. Some group I heard recently it says like everybody’s playing with the time but nobody’s playing the time.

Well you play in time. You don’t play the time. I could sit at the piano and walk around the room and come back and be right where you’re supposed to be. But the time is going on. Time doesn’t wait for anybody. And so the old guys, the drummers were more or less the timekeepers. They played a beat that went [scats]. But the bebop drummers, they were playing simple [scats]. They were playing counterpoint. And so the drums became just like another horn. And so everybody was interacting with each other contrapuntally. And so your time is supposed to be good enough to do that. If it’s not then you’ve got to work on that. You dig?
Yeah. Speaking of time, how’s our time? Okay. You are fun to talk to.
